answers.product: It's a software factory repo, for developers who want to have a sensible software factory from the get-go. Rather than treating every project as a bespoke effort, a software factory applies manufacturing-style repeatability to software delivery: templates, shared platforms, automated builds and tests, security controls, and deployment pipelines. The result is faster, more consistent delivery with fewer manual handoffs. It's a bit opinionated in the fact that it is built on Cloudflare, but it's a good way to get a SaaS off the ground running. Name: not really fixed. Generally it's a software factory, but what we have is more like a cf-saas-software-factory starter (I'm not affiliated with Cloudflare). What hurts today: right now people are just vibe coding, and/or don't know how to make their own software factory because the effort is ginormous on its own. What they use now: people are manually using skills and plugins and have to create their own environment; vibe coders wouldn't know how to do this. They may be using Matt Pocock's skills one by one, or similar tools one by one (also a set from a Y Combinator founder whose name the founder forgot).
answers.persona: Aimed at solo developers, startups, or people trying to create a framework inside their agency. Asked to pick one primary user, the founder said: I want to build for solo developer, startup team and agency lead. They want a software factory that they can start from. What stops them: right now they have nothing to build on top of. Others who may use it as a starting point: developers, vibe coders, product and UI/UX people who want something solid, or even new developers. There is no auth system, so nobody signs up. Who it is not for: not sure yet.
answers.scenario: Someone starting a SaaS, and they need the latest and greatest tools and workflows to get started. They scour through whatever GitHub links they can find and have to invoke each skill manually, making themselves a bottleneck rather than a software factory. How often: every time they have an app idea. Done looks like: they initialize their own factory and get to work. Where they are and on what device: not said.
answers.alsoAffected: Mostly teammates, on the DX side of things, then users of the said SaaS product. What each should feel: nothing separate was given; the founder gave only the product's overall feel.
answers.feel: The product should feel: simple, composable and succinct. It must never feel: complex, bloated, too much.
answers.goals: Three months (by 27 February 2027): 50 GitHub stars, people start using this, and 2 to 3 SaaS examples from our internal users. One year (by 27 November 2027): 1000 GitHub stars and 3 examples; hopefully we get traction and people start using this as a framework just like shadcn, where they can plug and play features.
answers.earns: Free and open source. The return: it speeds up our client work. Maybe a donation page; Buy Me a Coffee would be nice to have.
answers.antiGoals: Custom skills and custom plugins: we should be shipping workflows, not skills and plugins. We're not making anything new but creating a factory of how the skills and plugins work together. It's okay when skills are bundled with the workflow. Building outside Cloudflare: Cloudflare has the most amazing DX, as you can add services via wrangler and test it locally with the same API. Keeping true as a software factory.

output.markdown:
# Product foundation

## Product
A software factory starter, built on Cloudflare, for solo developers, startups and agency leads who want a sensible factory from the start instead of treating each project as bespoke work. The name is a working name: "software factory", or closer, "cf-saas-software-factory starter". The founder is not affiliated with Cloudflare.

## Problem
People vibe code, or they cannot build their own software factory because the effort is ginormous. Today they invoke skills and plugins by hand and build their own environment. They may use Matt Pocock's skills one by one, or similar tools one by one. They have nothing to build on top of, and each person becomes the bottleneck instead of a factory.

## Persona
Solo developer, startup team and agency lead, all wanting a software factory they can start from. The agency lead wants a framework inside the agency. What stops them: they have nothing to build on top of.

## Core scenario
Someone has an app idea and starts a SaaS. They need the latest and greatest tools and workflows. Today they search GitHub links and invoke each skill by hand. This happens every time they have an app idea. Done: they initialize their own factory and get to work.

## Also affected
Teammates, on the developer experience side. Then users of the SaaS products built this way. See Open.

## Not for
See Open.

## Feel
Simple, composable, succinct. Never complex, bloated or too much.

## Goals
1. By 27 February 2027: 50 GitHub stars.
2. By 27 February 2027: people start using this, and 2 to 3 SaaS examples from our internal users.
3. By 27 November 2027: 1000 GitHub stars and 3 examples. Hope for traction, with people using it as a framework like shadcn, plugging in features.

Earns by: free and open source; the return is faster client work for us. Maybe a donation page; Buy Me a Coffee would be nice to have.

## Anti-goals
1. Custom skills and custom plugins. We ship workflows, not skills and plugins. We make nothing new; we build a factory for how existing skills and plugins work together. Skills bundled with a workflow are fine.
2. Building outside Cloudflare. Cloudflare has the best developer experience: add services via wrangler and test locally with the same API. This keeps it a true software factory.

## Assumptions
- People want a whole factory, not single skills. Not yet proven.

## Open
- Product: the name is not fixed.
- Problem: the Y Combinator founder's skill set the founder meant is unnamed; the founder forgot the name.
- Persona: asked for one primary user, the founder named three (solo developer, startup team, agency lead). Which one comes first is not chosen.
- Persona: developers, vibe coders, product and UI/UX people and new developers may use it as a starting point; whether they are users is not said. Vibe coders are named in Problem as unable to build a factory themselves.
- Core scenario: where the user is and on what device is not said.
- Also affected: what teammates and SaaS users should feel is not said; only the product's overall feel was given.
- Not for: not sure yet.
- Goals: "people start using this" has no number or measure.
- Goals: 2 to 3 examples at three months and 3 at one year barely differ; the one-year example target may be too low or the three-month one unclear.
- Goals: no number is set for donations, and the factory's effect on client work has no measure.
- Assumptions: no test is set for whether people want a whole factory.

questions.question: Which one user do you build and write for first: solo developer, startup team or agency lead?
questions.why: The three want different things (speed, team workflow, a framework to impose on others), so the scenario, Feel and Not for cannot be pinned down until one comes first.

questions.question: Where is the person and what are they doing at the moment they decide to start a factory instead of one more bespoke project?
questions.why: Without a place and a trigger, one reader pictures a weekend side project and another a client kickoff, and the Done state means different things for each.
options: Alone, new idea at a laptop

questions.question: Who should this turn away: people who will not use Cloudflare, people who want no coding at all, or no one yet?
questions.why: The Cloudflare anti-goal already implies a boundary, and naming it keeps wrong-fit sign-ups from becoming stars that never become users.

questions.question: What number counts as 'people start using this' by 27 February 2027?
questions.why: Goal 2 has no measure, so on that date nobody could say whether it was met.

questions.question: What should the 27 November 2027 example target be, given 2 to 3 are due nine months earlier?
questions.why: Goal 3 asks for 3 examples where goal 2 already asks for 2 to 3, so it adds nothing and cannot show traction.

questions.question: How will you measure that the factory makes your own client work faster?
questions.why: Earning is the return on free and open source, yet no goal measures it, so it cannot be checked on a date.

questions.question: Where is the line between a workflow with bundled skills (allowed) and a custom skill (banned)?
questions.why: Without a test, any new skill can be called part of a workflow, so the first anti-goal cannot rule anything out.
options: Glue code only, no skill prose

questions.question: Does 'building outside Cloudflare' ban non-Cloudflare services such as Stripe, or only other hosts?
questions.why: The template already uses outside services, so a reviewer cannot judge a new feature until the scope is clear.

questions.question: Should we rule out a hosted or paid version of the factory (a platform, dashboard or SaaS)?
questions.why: A team that wants revenue will be tempted to sell a hosted version, which conflicts with free, open source and a simple feel.
options: Yes, but paid support is fine

questions.question: What would you accept as proof that people want a whole factory rather than single skills?
questions.why: This is the assumption that ends the product if false, and no test is set, so the document cannot say when it is settled.
options: 10 people use it on a real app
5 teams adopt it in a month

questions.question: What evidence do you have that the problem is real: who has told you, or shown you, they hit it?
questions.why: Problem rests on the founder's own experience; naming even one real person or source decides whether it states a fact or a guess.

questions.question: Why would someone leave single skills, or a template like create-t3-app, for this factory?
questions.why: The alternatives are named but no reason to switch is given, and that reason is what the document's pitch must say.
